entries.title: How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026
entries.summary: The UK Amazon Quick User Group's 2026 roundup: three quarterly meetups, 150+ attendees, and customer stories from Arriva, Carsa, and Propulse Lab on using agentic AI and Amazon Quick to turn data into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026

The Amazon Quick User Group – United Kingdom is a community of Amazon Quick users in the United Kingdom who meet quarterly to exchange knowledge, share best practices, learn through hands-on sessions, and discuss their experiences using the service. These user groups function as collaborative forums where members learn, connect, and innovate together.

Whether you’re already using Amazon Quick or just getting started, we’d love for you to join the UK Amazon Quick User Group and become part of a growing community that’s redefining how organizations make decisions with data. In this post, we’re thrilled to share our 2026 yearly roundup, highlighting all three quarterly meetups that have taken place since the group’s launch and the momentum that has followed. The events drew more than 150 attendees, and the energy in the room, fueled by agentic AI and the potential of Amazon Quick, was clear. Across industries, customers are using Amazon Quick to turn data chaos into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth. Their work spans real-time incident management, eliminating dashboard sprawl with governed data layers, and automating most support workflows with AI.

Why Amazon Quick user groups matter

The UK Amazon Quick User Group is a local community of Amazon Quick users who come together quarterly to share knowledge, best practices, and experiences with the service. Amazon Quick user groups serve as collaborative forums where members can:

  • Learn and share – Exchange real-world insights about the capabilities of Amazon Quick, from interactive dashboards and data storytelling to agentic AI-powered automations and custom agents. Members share what works, what doesn’t, and new approaches that drive results.
  • Network – Connect with regional professionals who are solving similar use cases with Amazon Quick for enterprise AI applications, data analytics, and workplace productivity.
  • Problem-solve – Tackle challenges collaboratively by discussing solutions and use cases across different industries and business contexts.
  • Stay updated – Get firsthand knowledge about new features, updates, and emerging best practices directly from peers and experts.
  • Build community – Foster a local support network that complements the broader Amazon Quick community, with trusted contacts who understand UK market and business context.

Event overview

Over three quarterly meetups this year, the UK community spent real time with Amazon Quick. Not slide decks about it, actual time building with it. People created Amazon Quick custom chat agents for their teams without writing code. They tried Amazon Quick Desktop running on their own laptops, connected to local files and using a connector to access Outlook. They also used Amazon Quick Apps to turn a plain-language description into a working web application. The workshops had attendees automating processes with Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate, while Amazon Quick Research showed how it significantly cuts down the time spent on research. The Amazon Quick chat agent tied it together, an assistant that connects to tools, data and takes actions on your behalf. Every quarter, the sessions got more practical and the questions from the room got sharper.

What a typical event looks like

All three events were held at the Amazon UK Corporate Office in Shoreditch, London. By 9:45 AM, the room is already buzzing. People reconnect over coffee, swap updates from the last quarter, and newcomers get pulled into conversations before the day even officially begins.

From there, the energy carries through the full agenda: customers share real stories about what they’ve built with Amazon Quick, product leads walk through the latest updates, and panels spark the kind of back-and-forth you don’t get from a webinar. The 75-minute hands-on workshop is where it really comes alive, with attendees rolling up their sleeves in provisioned sandbox accounts and experimenting together. By the time we close with a feedback session, the room feels more like a working group than an audience.

The format has shifted each quarter. Q1 leaned more on introductions and demos because the group was meeting for the first time. By Q2, we added an icebreaker quiz, and ran a focused workshop on Quick Flows and automation. For Q3 we brought in a specialist panel, a group quiz, and a networking slot at the end. That last one came about because people were already staying behind to talk after the close, so we stopped packing up around them and put it in the schedule.

What customers shared

Customer stories have been part of the community from the start. Each speaker brought a different problem into the room, showing how teams are applying Quick in very different environments.

At the first event, the conversation centered on getting insight into the hands of the people who need it. At Arriva UK Trains, critical data wasn’t reaching the people who needed it most. Train and station managers were constantly on the move, relying solely on their work mobiles. Sofia Bourika’s team built dynamic, role-based dashboards with mobile-friendly views and introduced pixel perfect reports automatically delivered through scheduled email, giving managers immediate visibility of incidents and performance. The result: faster decisions, better incident management, and a stronger data-driven culture across the organization.

By Q2, the discussion had moved toward a different challenge: getting the foundations right before introducing more AI and automation. At Carsa, a used-car retailer, analytics functioned like a service desk. Question in, dashboard out. The same question gave different answers. It wasn’t a data problem. It was a definitions problem. Tobi Daramola’s team at Carsa fixed this by building a single governed data layer, with metrics defined once and consumed by Amazon Quick and AI assistants alike. As a result, they removed 50 percent of dashboards while surfacing more data. Customer satisfaction (CSAT) scores moved 10 percent in 30 days, complaints same-day close rate jumped 20 percent, and AI on the layer cut recurring tasks from 45 minutes to 5.

Q3 brought the conversation further into automation and agentic workflows. Propulse Lab, a Swiss operating system for B2C subscription businesses, was handling 1 million support tickets a year. Their teams were stuck firefighting instead of driving growth. After deploying a multi-agent AI pipeline in Amazon Quick Automate, built from their best past customer service interactions, they cut request handling from 7 minutes to 70 seconds. The pipeline also automated 80 percent of routine workflows.

“What was once a cost centre became a growth engine – their product managers now own the entire system without writing a single line of code, and their support teams focus on proactive, revenue-driving conversations instead.”

— Guirec Lecointre, Growth Operations Specialist, Propulse Lab

The use cases vary widely, and that’s exactly the point. Rather than presenting a single vision for Amazon Quick, practitioners show what they’ve tried against real business problems, from governed analytics and frontline reporting to automation and AI. That shifts the conversation in the room. Attendees ask direct questions about implementation, adoption, and what didn’t work. Speakers share the practical lessons behind the finished solution. People leave with ideas they can apply to their own organizations, not just another customer story.

From presentations to participation

Attendees changed across the three events. A listen-and-learn turned into building meaningful relationships by Q3. People were new to the group and new to each other. By Q2, the icebreaker quiz loosened things up early. The feedback sessions got more specific too: instead of “this was great,” people were requesting topics and offering to contribute.

Q3 pushes this further. Sofia Bourika, who joined the leadership team early on and presented the Arriva customer story at the first event, came up with an icebreaker called “What Are You Proud Of?”, attendees share something they’ve built with Amazon Quick. We’ve already got someone who was previously sitting in the audience volunteering to present their work. That kind of shift, from attending to contributing, took three events to happen, but it happened. Q3 also introduced a new segment, the Amazon Quick specialist panel. Questions were pre-collected from the audience and posed to an invited specialist, who brought real depth to the answers and shared first-hand experience of working with attendees’ customers. It sparked a different kind of thinking in the room, with the audience connecting the dots between the specialist’s insights and their own day-to-day challenges.

Our community stayed connected all year. Our LinkedIn group had weekly contributions and our email lists encouraged involvement.

Collective impact in action

A huge thank you to our dedicated AWS Partner, Data Reply, whose consistent contributions and thought leadership have been instrumental in making every UK user group meetup a success.

Our UK leadership team led us to reach every milestone:

Liam Yusuph, AI and Data Delivery Lead, Data Reply

Priyanka Bettaswamygowda, Solutions Architect, AWS

Sahar Shahbaz, Data Analyst, Data Reply

Sofia Bourika, Lead BI Developer, Arriva

Tobi Daramola, Senior Data and Analytics Lead, Carsa

Ali Hayat, AV Support Associate, Amazon

Lam Phan, BI Developer, AWS

Rikhi Singh, ADC Engineer, AWS

Amazon Quick Community resources

The Amazon Quick Community website has tens of thousands of members and thousands of searchable questions. It also offers over 600 learning resources on accelerating your productivity with agentic AI and Amazon Quick.

“The Quick Community is about learning together and building connections. It’s where users at any skill level can find help, learn something new, and meet others. What I love most about the Quick Community is how genuinely helpful everyone is. It’s a place that reveals possibilities you wouldn’t have thought to explore on your own, where you stumble into people working on projects and use cases, you’d never even think to ask about, and suddenly your world gets a whole lot bigger.”

— Kristin Mandia, Sr. Community Manager, AWS

Learning opportunities include approximately two free live online sessions per week, monthly feature update detailed and advanced automation sessions, and 4-hour Immersion Day workshops. AWS Solutions Architects, Product Managers, and subject matter experts are active on the platform and available for direct messaging. Kristin continues, “People jump in to help solve tricky problems, share their clever workarounds, and experiment with new ways to use Quick together.”

Key takeaways

A few themes came up consistently across the three events.

The format keeps changing because we listen

The Amazon Quick User Group UK runs on a set structure: an introduction, a product update, customer stories, a hands-on workshop, and a feedback session. But we’ve been adjusting it every quarter. Early on, we had the “What’s New with Quick” segment right after customer stories, and it broke the flow. People were engaged with how a real company was using the product, then we’d switch to feature announcements. We moved “What’s New” so the customer stories lead straight into the workshop, and the difference was noticeable. For Q3, we added an interactive quiz to get more back-and-forth going in the room. Attendees also called out the overall format and pacing, and the chance to meet new people. As one first-time attendee put it, “the networking opportunities were excellent… I thoroughly enjoyed the day!”.

Customers present, not us

At least one customer shares how they use Amazon Quick at each event. Across three events, we’ve had Carsa, Arriva, Propulse Lab, and a few other customers on stage. After the very first event, one of the clearest pieces of feedback was that people wanted more customer speakers. That told us we were on the right track. The sessions work because the audience is hearing from peers who face similar problems, not from someone trying to sell them something. The impact goes beyond the event itself. Attendees said the customer stories showed them new ways to use the tools and started useful discussions about return on investment (ROI). One attendee told us a customer session “has already prompted a lot of conversation internally” at their organization.

The workshop is where it clicks

Every event has a hands-on workshop, and people consistently tell us it’s the part they get the most out of. There’s a gap between watching someone demo a product and sitting down with it yourself. That gap is where most attendees say Amazon Quick starts to make sense for what they’re trying to do. We know it lands because the most common question afterwards is whether they can keep access to the workshop environment so they can carry on experimenting on their own.

Conclusion

The success of this year’s meetups is a testament to every single member who showed up, shared their knowledge, and contributed to making this community what it is today. As we look ahead, we’re more energized than ever to keep this momentum going and continue pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with Amazon Quick.

Get involved

To learn more about Amazon Quick and connect with the community:

  • Join the UK Amazon Quick User Group on LinkedIn.
  • Join the Amazon Quick Community to learn agentic AI together and access over 600 learning resources.
  • Explore Amazon Bedrock for additional generative AI capabilities.
  • Register for the next UK Amazon Quick User Group meetup: January 28, 2027.
  • Not in the UK? Attend a meetup in Austin, Phoenix, Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles, New York City, or Munich/DACH.
  • Complete the leadership interest form to start an Amazon Quick User Group in your city.

For questions about the event or the Amazon Quick Community, Kristin Mandia, Sr. Community Manager, Amazon Quick Community and User Group program, at kmandia@amazon.com.

entries.title: Building intent-driven UI testing with Amazon Nova Act
entries.summary: Epsilon's Agentic Platform team delivers UI testing as a managed, multi-tenant service built on Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool. Tests are written in plain English and run on browsers managed by AWS, giving every product team resilient, intent-driven testing with zero per-team infrastructure overhead.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Building intent-driven UI testing with Amazon Nova Act

To scale intent-driven UI testing across its product teams, Epsilon, a data, technology, and marketing-services company and part of Publicis Groupe, turned to Amazon Nova Act. With hundreds of millions of consumer profiles and thousands of brand relationships, Epsilon needed UI testing that could keep pace with rapid application changes. The solution could not create maintenance overhead for every product team.

Within Epsilon, the Agentic Platform team (50 engineers) builds shared infrastructure so other product teams can build, deploy, govern, and run AI agents safely. With this shared platform, teams get a skills-based agent builder. They also get federated identity and pre-flight authorization, Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, and cross-account provisioning. When a product team wants to adopt AI tooling, they get capabilities without additional configuration and without re-solving identity, security, browser infrastructure, or model integration on their own.

One of those managed capabilities is UI testing. With Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Epsilon’s platform team could deliver resilient, intent-driven testing as a service to teams on the platform.

In this post, we walk through Epsilon’s architecture for delivering UI testing as a managed platform service, show the core Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration code, highlight a concrete 18-step test workflow, and share best practices and measured results.

The challenge: Enhancing coverage, not replacing what works

Epsilon’s existing UI testing practice was not broken. The team maintained a Playwright-based regression suite that validated functionality across their web applications, and it worked well. Playwright remains their regression backbone today.

The opportunity Epsilon identified was additive, not corrective:

  • Scripted Playwright tests are effective for deterministic regression checks. However, they are tightly coupled to selectors and page structure. Cosmetic UI changes can break them even when the underlying functionality is sound.
  • Multiple product teams needed full testing coverage against their own applications. Standing up browser infrastructure, managing dependencies, and integrating with identity systems per team created duplicative effort.
  • The platform team wanted UI testing to be a managed capability that fit their existing agent model, not a custom CLI that every onboarded team had to operate.

The goal: layer intent-based testing on top of the existing Playwright regression suite. Deliver it as a multi-tenant platform service so that each Epsilon product team could consume through the same API surface they used for every other agent capability.

Why Epsilon chose Amazon Nova Act and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool

Epsilon evaluated options against two requirements: natural-language test authoring (to complement selector-based Playwright tests) and managed browser infrastructure (to fit their multi-tenant platform model). With Amazon Nova Act combined with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, Epsilon could address both.

  • Natural-language steps. Test steps are plain-English instructions executed by Nova Act. They are resilient to cosmetic UI changes and readable by non-engineers. A step like “Confirm the rewards balance is visible” ages far better than a brittle CSS selector.
  • AWS managed, ephemeral browser sessions. With Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, teams get isolated browser instances with no binaries to ship and no display server to maintain. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool also offers live view for human observation or takeover (useful for CAPTCHAs or multi-factor authentication), session recording to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and AWS CloudTrail audit, all without additional configuration.
  • AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM)-based authentication. With Nova Act, you can authenticate through the standard AWS credential chain (the task role). This fits Epsilon’s existing security model without distributing separate API keys.
  • Cross-account friendly. With Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, you can slot into your existing AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) AssumeRole provisioning. Each onboarded team can run tests inside their own AWS account under a scoped role. This maintains isolation and auditability.

Epsilon chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool specifically because it eliminates the operational burden of managing browser binaries, display servers, and session lifecycle. The Agentic Platform team had no interest in owning that infrastructure.

The solution: Architecture and implementation

Epsilon’s solution has three main components: a platform API for creating workflows, a background task runner for executing them, and the Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration that drives the browser.

Platform architecture

Epsilon’s UI testing capability follows a clear pipeline:

  • A user creates a workflow through the platform API, specifying a 
    target_url
    and a list of natural-language steps.
  • On create, the platform registers a Nova Act workflow definition on AWS.
  • On execute, a background task runner (Celery, a Python framework for asynchronous job processing) opens an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool browser session. It runs each step through Nova Act over a Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) WebSocket (the standard interface for programmatically controlling Chromium browsers), including conditional logic (for example, “if a tour box appears, skip it”).
  • The system captures a screenshot per step, tracks pass/fail per step, computes an overall pass rate, and stores everything (results JSON, screenshots in Amazon S3, session ID).
  • A completion hook fires so the result is recorded back into the platform.

Figure 1 shows the layered architecture of Epsilon’s UI Testing Service. User requests flow from the Agent Cloud Frontend through an API Gateway with authentication and permission checks. The API layer (Django REST) exposes endpoints for workflows, executions, automation suites, and stats. The business logic layer includes a Workflow Manager, Execution Orchestrator, and Suite Coordinator. Test jobs are queued in Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) and picked up by the Runner Service running on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), which contains the Nova Act engine and a headless Chromium browser. Results, screenshots, trajectories, and HTML reports are stored in Amazon S3.

The capability is exposed as a standard agent (

ui-test-agent
) with two skills:
  • ui-test-recorder: Explore a scenario interactively and record natural-language steps.
  • ui-test-executor: Run recorded steps and return structured results.

Onboarded teams consume UI testing the same way they consume any other platform agent. No additional infrastructure to manage. The onboarding process is straightforward. The platform team provisions a cross-account IAM role for the new team, registers their target application URLs, and grants access to the 

ui-test-agent
through the existing platform API. From that point, teams create workflows, trigger executions, and retrieve results through the same interface they already use for other platform capabilities.

The core integration

The Nova Act + Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration is concise:

This pattern (open a managed browser session, connect through the CDP WebSocket, and drive actions with natural language) is the foundation. Epsilon wraps it with their platform’s multi-tenant orchestration, result capture, and observability layers.

Example: Automating the ‘Create an agent’ flow

To illustrate intent-based testing, here is a representative workflow from Epsilon’s platform. It exercises login, form entry, conditional handling, scrolling, and verification. The following steps highlight the differentiating patterns of Nova Act:

StepInstruction
1Type the username and choose Next
2Enter the password and choose Verify
3Navigate to Create Agent and select the Design a new specification card
4If an onboarding tour box appears, choose Skip Tour, then verify the correct page loaded
5Fill in the agent name and description fields
6Scroll down until the Goal Statement field is visible, then fill it in
7If the skills search box is not visible, scroll until it appears. Then search for and add a skill
8Choose Save, confirm the success prompt, navigate back, and verify the new agent appears in the list

Steps 4 and 7 demonstrate conditional logic: “if an element appears, handle it” and “if a target isn’t visible, scroll until it is.” These patterns would require explicit branching in a traditional framework. Nova Act handles them naturally through language understanding.

Runtime isolation

Epsilon runs UI tests in a dedicated runner service (a FastAPI sidecar) that pins 

nova-act
3.x with Workflow and IAM authentication support, plus the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool client. This keeps dependencies separate from the main backend so they don’t collide with the Strands agent stack. The worker falls back to in-process execution if the runner is disabled, providing resilience during deployments.

Best practices

Based on their experience building UI testing as a platform capability, the Epsilon team recommends:

1. Write steps as intent, not mechanics

Intent-based steps survive UI redesigns. Product managers and quality assurance (QA) leads who might not write code can review them directly.

2. Isolate the Nova Act runtime

Pin Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool dependencies in a dedicated service or container. Epsilon learned that the signing endpoint for Nova Act targets 

us-east-1
regardless of the browser session’s region. Running it in a separate service with its own dependency lockfile prevents hard-to-debug conflicts.

3. Reuse recorded trajectories to cut cost

Epsilon uses trajectory retries in draft state, saves the successful trajectory, and replays it in active state. Repeat runs skip redundant large language model (LLM) “thinking,” reducing both latency and cost for regression-style repeated executions.

4. Design for multi-tenancy from day one

Use cross-account AssumeRole with scoped IAM policies. Each tenant’s tests run under their own role in their own account. This provides isolation, auditability, and failure scope containment without custom infrastructure per team.

5. Lean on managed observability

With Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, teams get live view, session recording, and AWS CloudTrail integration. Epsilon uses these built-in capabilities instead of building custom observability, reducing maintenance and giving compliance teams familiar audit surfaces.

6. Account for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool viewport behavior

When prompting Nova Act steps, account for the browser viewport defaults of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool. Steps that reference scrolling (for example, “scroll down until the Goal Statement textbox is visible”) verify that Nova Act handles content in the lower portion of the page correctly.

Results and impact

Epsilon’s UI testing capability is operational across multiple teams, with the multi-tenant architecture proven in production.

DimensionAmazon Nova ActPlaywright (equivalent)
Lines authored18 natural-language steps~80-150 lines of code
Selector/DOM inspectionNoneRequired per interactive step
Authoring time (per workflow)~5-10 minutes~30-90 minutes
Effort ratioBaseline4-6x more effort

Here are the measured outcomes:

  • 4-6x faster test authoring (based on Epsilon’s internal benchmarks). A representative 18-step workflow took 5–10 minutes to author with Nova Act, compared to 30–90 minutes for the equivalent Playwright script (80–150 lines of code). Each interactive step in the Playwright script requires inspecting the DOM, choosing a stable selector, and coding explicit waits, assertions, and branching for conditional cases. Nova Act replaces that per-step overhead with 18 natural-language instructions and zero selector or DOM inspection, with conditional logic (such as the tour-box and scroll-until-visible steps) expressed in plain English.
  • 100 percent pass rate on trajectory replay (based on Epsilon’s internal benchmarks). After a workflow passes the initial explore phase (typically 4–5 prompt iterations), Epsilon saves the successful trajectory and replays it deterministically. Saved trajectories achieve a 100 percent pass rate across repeated runs.
  • Lower barrier to test authoring. Steps read like plain English. Team members beyond core test engineers can read, review, and propose tests, broadening ownership of quality.
